quiz.q: A 70-year-old (60 kg, CrCl 22 mL/min) needs enoxaparin to treat a DVT. Which regimen is appropriate?
quiz.explain: With CrCl below 30 mL/min the treatment dose is 1 mg/kg once daily, because enoxaparin accumulates in renal impairment. Consider anti-Xa monitoring or unfractionated heparin when renal function is unstable.

quiz.q: A COPD patient on theophylline needs a macrolide. Which choice is least likely to raise theophylline levels?
quiz.explain: Erythromycin and clarithromycin inhibit theophylline metabolism and can cause toxicity. Azithromycin has no clinically important effect, so it is preferred; otherwise monitor levels.

quiz.q: Day 3 of IV levofloxacin 750 mg daily for pneumonia: afebrile for 48 h, stable, eating normally. Best recommendation?
options: Switch to oral levofloxacin 750 mg once daily
Switch to oral at double the dose
quiz.explain: Levofloxacin is almost 100% bioavailable, so the oral dose equals the IV dose. Switch once the patient is clinically stable and can absorb oral drugs.

quiz.q: A ward patient (not ICU, not ventilated, normal coagulation, no GI bleed history) receives IV pantoprazole 'for prophylaxis'. Best recommendation?
options: Switch to an oral PPI for 3 months
Stop it: no stress-ulcer prophylaxis indication
quiz.explain: Stress-ulcer prophylaxis is indicated mainly for ICU patients with risk factors such as mechanical ventilation or coagulopathy. Unnecessary PPIs add cost and raise the risk of C. difficile and pneumonia.

quiz.q: Which approach to vancomycin monitoring is preferred for serious MRSA infections?
options: Fixed 1 g every 12 h without levels
quiz.explain: The 2020 consensus guideline prefers AUC-guided dosing: it is as effective as high troughs with less kidney injury.

quiz.q: A patient on sertraline is started on linezolid. What is the main interaction risk?
quiz.explain: Linezolid is a weak MAO inhibitor. With SSRIs it can cause serotonin syndrome, so consider an alternative or monitor closely for agitation, tremor, hyperthermia and clonus.

quiz.q: Levofloxacin 750 mg every 24 h is ordered; CrCl is 35 mL/min. What is the correct adjustment?
quiz.explain: For CrCl 20-49 mL/min the 750 mg regimen becomes 750 mg every 48 h, which keeps the high peak that fluoroquinolones need.

quiz.q: A patient on a heparin infusion for pulmonary embolism also has enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily on the chart. What is the problem?
options: No problem: prophylaxis plus treatment is standard
quiz.explain: Two anticoagulants at the same time sharply increase bleeding risk. Prophylactic enoxaparin must stop when therapeutic heparin starts.

quiz.q: Hypokalaemia does not improve despite IV potassium. What should be checked and corrected first?
quiz.explain: Low magnesium increases renal potassium loss, so potassium stays low until magnesium is replaced.
quiz.source: Huang & Kuo, J Am Soc Nephrol 2007

quiz.q: Systemic steroids for a COPD exacerbation: what does GOLD recommend?
options: IV methylprednisolone 125 mg every 6 h for 10 days
quiz.explain: A short course of prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days works as well as longer courses, with fewer adverse effects.

quiz.q: A patient stable on warfarin (INR 2.5) is started on fluconazole. What do you expect?
options: INR falls - increase the warfarin dose
INR rises - check INR within 3-5 days and consider a dose reduction
quiz.explain: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9, the main pathway for S-warfarin, so the INR can rise sharply. Monitor closely and reduce the dose if needed.

quiz.q: What is the usual adult ceftriaxone dose for bacterial meningitis?
quiz.explain: Meningitis needs high CSF levels: 2 g every 12 hours (4 g/day), versus 1-2 g daily for most other infections.

quiz.q: Potassium 7.1 mmol/L with peaked T waves. Which drug is given first?
quiz.explain: Calcium stabilises the heart muscle within minutes. It does not lower potassium, so insulin with glucose and other measures follow.

quiz.q: Below which eGFR is metformin contraindicated?
quiz.explain: Metformin is contraindicated below eGFR 30. Starting is not recommended at 30-45, and the dose is reviewed when eGFR falls below 45.

quiz.q: Which combination carries the highest risk of QT prolongation?
quiz.explain: Both drugs prolong the QT interval. Check the ECG, potassium and magnesium, or choose alternatives.

quiz.q: Which electrolyte disturbance increases the risk of digoxin toxicity most?
quiz.explain: Low potassium increases digoxin binding to Na/K-ATPase, so toxicity can occur even at 'normal' levels.

quiz.q: A COPD patient uses tiotropium daily and also has regular ipratropium nebules four times a day. Best recommendation?
options: Stop the regular ipratropium: duplicate anticholinergic
quiz.explain: Both are muscarinic antagonists, so adding regular ipratropium to tiotropium adds side effects, not benefit. Use a short-acting beta-agonist for relief.

quiz.q: A patient on clopidogrel needs a PPI. Which is preferred?
quiz.explain: Omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19, which activates clopidogrel. Pantoprazole has little effect.

quiz.q: Flushing and itching appear during a vancomycin infusion, blood pressure is normal. What should be done?
options: Stop vancomycin permanently - it is an allergy
Slow the infusion (no faster than 10 mg/min) and consider an antihistamine
Give the next dose as an IV push
Switch to oral vancomycin for bacteraemia
quiz.explain: This is an infusion-rate reaction (vancomycin flushing syndrome), not a true allergy. A slower infusion usually prevents it.

quiz.q: VTE prophylaxis with enoxaparin for a medical patient with CrCl 25 mL/min: what dose?
quiz.explain: With CrCl below 30 mL/min the prophylactic dose is 30 mg once daily. Unfractionated heparin is an alternative.

No indication: Ask 'what is this for?' for every drug. Stress-ulcer prophylaxis outside ICU risk criteria and continued empiric antibiotics are common examples.
Duplication: Look across routes and names: IV plus oral PPI, two anticoagulants, or two drugs of the same class under different brands.
Untreated indication: Admission medication reconciliation finds omitted home medicines such as inhalers, antiepileptics and antihypertensives.
Prophylaxis needed: Assess VTE risk (for example Padua score 4 or more in medical patients) and bleeding risk before recommending prophylaxis.
Add-on therapy needed: State the goal the current therapy is missing (for example blood pressure or glucose target) when recommending an add-on.
Ineffective / better option: Review culture results at 48-72 h and de-escalate or switch to the narrowest effective antibiotic.
Contraindication / risk factor: Clarify the allergy type: a remote rash is different from anaphylaxis. Many 'penicillin allergies' can take cephalosporins.
Route / dosage form: Highly bioavailable drugs (levofloxacin, linezolid, metronidazole, fluconazole) switch IV to oral at the same dose once the patient is stable.
Interaction: Name the mechanism - CYP, QT, serotonergic or additive bleeding. It tells you the fix: another drug, a dose change, or monitoring.
Dose too high: Check weight and kidney function before calling a dose high: most labels base renal dosing on Cockcroft-Gault CrCl.
Dose too low: Severe infections often need loading doses (for example vancomycin 20-35 mg/kg) even when maintenance doses are reduced.
Frequency / interval: Beta-lactams depend on time above MIC: stretching the interval lowers efficacy even if the daily dose is the same.
Duration: Community-acquired pneumonia usually needs 5 days when the patient is clinically stable.
Renal / hepatic dose: Write the CrCl you used and the source table in the details, so the physician can check it quickly.
Monitoring needed: A good monitoring recommendation states the test, the timing and the target - for example 'INR in 3 days, target 2-3'.
Adverse reaction: Report suspected adverse reactions to your national pharmacovigilance centre and record them in the patient file.

case.title: Case of the month: the theophylline level
case.text: A 68-year-old man with a COPD exacerbation was on oral theophylline. Clarithromycin was started for pneumonia. On day 3 he had nausea, palpitations and a theophylline level of 24 mg/L.
case.lesson: Clarithromycin inhibits theophylline metabolism. The pharmacist recommended holding theophylline, rechecking the level, and switching to azithromycin. Check every new antibiotic against drugs with a narrow therapeutic range.
